title: Accounting Records
tagline: Journals, ledgers, the cash book and the trial balance — what each record is, what it is for, and how one becomes the next, without entries or calculations.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original BoardPrep study material written against the CISCE ICSE Commercial Applications syllabus registered in this subject’s baseline (Examination Year 2027 and 2028 documents as reproduced by AglaSem, Scribd and Oswal Publishers; cisce.org returned 403). No board examination paper was consulted, every question is original practice, no figure is presented as an official statistic, and — as the syllabus itself requires — no question asks the student to record accounting entries or perform accounting calculations.

overview.intro: Unit 4(d) completes the syllabus with the four records: journals, ledgers, the cash book and the trial balance. The syllabus is explicit that only a simple understanding is required and that no questions will be set on recording entries or calculations, so this chapter teaches each record as a link in a chain — transaction happens, it is written in the journal, posted into the ledger, summarised by the trial balance, and cash movements are captured in the cash book throughout. Understanding what each record contains and what it is for is the entire requirement, and it is also what makes a student able to explain why an accountant needs four documents instead of one.

learn.title: The journal: the book of original entry

blocks.text: The journal is where a business writes its transactions down first, in the order in which they happen. Each entry states the date, the accounts affected, what was received and what was given, and a short narration explaining the transaction — for example, that goods were bought on credit from a named supplier. Because it captures events at the moment they occur, it is called the book of original entry, and its virtue is completeness in sequence: if every transaction is written here as it arises, nothing can be omitted later without leaving a visible gap. The journal also carries amounts on two sides for each event, which is the practical form of the rule that total debits equal total credits. For examination purposes the requirement is understanding: a student should be able to say what the journal is (the book of original entry), what it contains (date, accounts, amounts and a narration), what it is for (recording transactions in order of occurrence), and why a business needs it (to have a complete chronological story before the information is sorted by account). The syllabus excludes preparing entries, so no example here asks for one.

learn.title: The ledger: one account for every heading

blocks.text: The journal tells the story event by event; the ledger sorts it by subject. It is a book containing a separate account for each heading the business uses — cash, purchases, sales, each supplier, each customer, capital, rent and the rest — and into these accounts the journal’s entries are transferred, an operation called posting. The point of the rearrangement is that a heading answers a question the journal cannot: how much is owed to this particular supplier, what is the balance of cash, how much was spent on rent this year. Each account shows what it received on one side and what it was given on the other, and at any date the difference between the two sides is that account’s balance. The ledger is therefore the firm’s memory organised for retrieval rather than for sequence, and it is the source from every later summary is drawn. The syllabus asks only for understanding, so a student should describe the ledger as the book of final entry holding accounts under headings, explain posting as the transfer from journal to ledger, and state that balances drawn from it feed the trial balance and the final statements.

items.text: Every purchase from every supplier appears in the journal; all of them appear together in the purchases account of the ledger.
items.note: Chronology becomes category — the same information reorganised to answer a different question.

items.text: A customer’s account in the ledger shows what was sold to him and what he has paid.
items.note: A running balance per person, which no chronological list can give at a glance.

learn.title: The cash book and the trial balance

blocks.text: The cash book is the record devoted to money in and money out — every receipt of cash and every payment made is entered in it, and it doubles as the cash account itself, so its balance states what the business holds at any moment. Firms maintain it separately from the journal because cash is the most frequent and most vulnerable transaction type: a dedicated book gives an immediate answer to how much is available, shows the pattern of receipts and payments, and makes shortfalls visible quickly. Bank transactions are recorded alongside, which is why the cash book covers both cash in hand and bank balances. The trial balance comes last in the chain. It is a list drawn from the ledger of every account with its closing balance, arranged so that the debit balances stand in one column and the credit balances in another, with totals at the foot. Its purpose is a check: if the two columns agree, the arithmetic of the recording process so far is in agreement, since equal debits and credits at every stage must produce equal totals here. What it does not prove is equally important to state — agreement does not guarantee that every transaction was recorded, recorded in the right account, or recorded at the correct amount; it proves only that the debit-credit equality has been maintained.

learn.title: Why the business needs four records and not one

blocks.text: A single book cannot answer four different questions at once, which is why the syllabus teaches four records. The journal answers what happened and in what order, and its completeness makes it the evidence of record. The ledger answers what the position of each heading is, and its balances are what anyone actually asks for — how much cash, how much owed, how much owing. The cash book answers how much money is available today, a question urgent enough to deserve its own book. The trial balance answers whether the whole process still adds up, and it does so before anyone attempts to read results from the accounts. Each record is also a control on the previous ones: entries omitted from the journal cannot appear in the ledger, mispostings disturb the trial balance, and a cash book balance that disagrees with the ledger’s cash account points straight at an error. The examination requirement remains understanding, so a strong answer describes each record’s content and purpose and then shows the order in which information flows — transaction to journal to ledger to trial balance, with the cash book running alongside — without preparing a single entry, exactly as the syllabus directs.

keyPoints: The journal is the book of original entry, recording transactions in order with a narration.
Each entry affects two accounts with equal amounts, so the totals remain equal.
The ledger is the book of final entry, holding one account under each heading.
Posting is the transfer of entries from the journal into their ledger accounts.
The cash book records every cash and bank receipt and payment and shows the balance available.
The trial balance lists account balances in debit and credit columns with totals.
An agreeing trial balance proves the arithmetic consistency of the records.
Agreement does not prove that every transaction was recorded or recorded correctly.
The four records form a chain: transaction → journal → ledger → trial balance, with the cash book alongside.
The syllabus requires understanding of these records only — no entries and no calculations.
examFocus: “What is a journal?” — name it as the book of original entry, list what an entry contains, and state its purpose.
“Distinguish journal and ledger” — chronology against category, original entry against final entry, and the posting link between them.
“What does a trial balance show?” — the two columns and what agreement proves, plus one thing it does not prove.

questions.prompt: The book in which transactions are first recorded in order of occurrence is the:
questions.explanation: The journal is the book of original entry — transactions are written into it as they happen, before being sorted into ledger accounts.
questions.commonMistake: The ledger is the book of final entry; it receives what the journal records.

questions.prompt: The ledger differs from the journal mainly because it:
options: Organises transactions by heading instead of by date
Is prepared before the transaction occurs
questions.answer: Organises transactions by heading instead of by date
questions.explanation: The journal preserves chronology while the ledger sorts the same information into one account per heading, which is what allows balances to be read off per supplier or per expense.
questions.commonMistake: Two-column listing belongs to the trial balance, not the ledger.

questions.prompt: When a trial balance agrees, it proves that:
options: Total debit balances equal total credit balances in the records so far
No account has been used wrongly
The business has made a profit
questions.answer: Total debit balances equal total credit balances in the records so far
questions.explanation: Agreement demonstrates that the debit-credit equality has been maintained arithmetically; completeness and correct classification are separate matters it cannot confirm.
questions.commonMistake: Agreement is not correctness — that distinction is a standard examination point.

questions.prompt: A record that answers “how much cash is available in the business today?” is the:
questions.explanation: The cash book records every receipt and payment of cash and bank money, so its current balance answers the availability question directly.
questions.commonMistake: The ledger’s cash account gives a balance too, but the cash book keeps the running record day to day.

questions.prompt: The brief written explanation that accompanies an entry in a journal is called a ______.
questions.explanation: The narration states what the transaction was, so the entry remains understandable to anyone reading the book later.
questions.commonMistake: Do not write “description” — the standard term the syllabus expects is narration.

questions.prompt: State two purposes of the journal.
questions.answer: It records transactions in the order in which they occur, so a complete chronological story of the business is preserved as evidence. And it states each transaction on two sides with equal amounts, which applies the debit-credit rule at the moment of recording and keeps the totals equal from the start.
questions.explanation: Both purposes come from the journal’s position at the beginning of the chain — capture in sequence and capture in balance.
questions.commonMistake: Do not say the journal shows balances; balances are read from the ledger.

questions.prompt: What is posting, and why is it necessary?
questions.answer: Posting is the transfer of the information from a journal entry into the relevant account in the ledger. It is necessary because the journal records events in the order they happened, which cannot answer questions about a particular heading; posting reorganises the same information so that all activity relating to cash, or to one supplier, stands together and a balance can be arrived at.
questions.explanation: The term is defined and then justified by the change of organisation it accomplishes, which is the reasoning behind having two books.
questions.commonMistake: Posting is journal to ledger, never ledger to journal.

questions.prompt: Describe the trial balance and explain what its agreement does and does not prove.
questions.answer: The trial balance is a list prepared from the ledger at a stated date showing the balance of every account, with debit balances in one column and credit balances in another and totals at the foot of each column. What its agreement proves is arithmetic consistency: because every transaction has been recorded with equal debits and credits at each stage, the totals of the two columns must be equal, and if they are, the recording process has not disturbed the debit-credit equality. What it does not prove is just as important. It cannot show that a transaction was recorded at all — an omitted transaction is simply absent from both columns. It cannot show that an entry was made in the correct account, since posting to the wrong heading keeps both columns equal. Nor can it show that an amount was entered at the correct value, or that a transaction was recorded twice, because equal errors on both sides cancel out in the totals. The trial balance is therefore a necessary check before results are read from the accounts, not a certificate that the accounts are correct.
questions.explanation: The structure is described, then both halves of the question are answered with named exceptions, which is the complete understanding the syllabus requires.
questions.commonMistake: Do not say agreement proves the accounts are error-free — list at least one error it cannot detect.

questions.prompt: Explain the relationship between the journal, the ledger and the trial balance with the help of a simple description of a transaction’s journey.
questions.answer: The three records form a chain in which each prepares the material the next uses. Take a purchase of goods on credit from a supplier. The transaction is first written in the journal with the date, the accounts affected, equal amounts on both sides and a narration stating that goods were bought on credit from the named supplier — this is the original record. The two entries are then posted into the ledger: the purchases account receives the purchase amount, and the supplier’s account shows the amount now owed to him, so chronology has been converted into category. At the end of the period, the balances of all ledger accounts — including purchases and the supplier’s balance — are extracted into the trial balance, where debit balances stand in one column and credit balances in another. If the columns agree, the journey has preserved equal debits and credits at every stage. The cash book runs alongside, recording any payment when the supplier is finally settled. Thus one transaction is captured once in the journal, sorted once in the ledger, checked once in the trial balance, and no stage repeats the work of another.
questions.explanation: A single transaction is followed through all three records with the function of each stated, which demonstrates the relationship rather than describing the books separately.
questions.commonMistake: Do not omit posting — the link that makes the chain a chain is the transfer between journal and ledger.

questions.prompt: A firm finds that its trial balance agrees but its profit is far lower than expected, and some expenses seem missing. Explain how such a situation is possible, describing what each of the four records contributes to finding the answer.
questions.answer: Agreement of the trial balance is compatible with missing expenses because it tests only equality, not completeness. If a bill for electricity was never written in the journal, no debit reaches the ledger, no balance reaches either column, and the totals still agree — the omission is invisible to the equality check. The same applies if the expense was posted to the wrong account, entered at too small an amount, or recorded twice with an equal and opposite error. The four records locate the fault in sequence. The journal is examined first, since it is the chronological evidence: listing the period’s transactions in date order shows whether the electricity bill appears at all, and its narration reveals what each entry was meant to be. The ledger is examined next because it sorts by heading — the electricity account shows what was posted to it, and the absence of an entry there, while the cash book shows the payment going out, exposes the omission precisely. The cash book itself is the strongest witness in this case: every payment of money is recorded in it, so a payment with no corresponding expense in the ledger points directly to a posting error. Finally the trial balance is re-read not as proof but as a starting point — its agreement tells the accountant the arithmetic is intact, so the search can be confined to completeness and classification rather than to addition. The sequence shows why the syllabus keeps four records: each answers a question the others cannot, and together they turn an unexplained profit figure into a located entry.
questions.explanation: The answer explains the logical gap in the trial balance with named examples, then assigns a specific diagnostic role to each of the four records — the applied understanding unit 4 is built to produce.
questions.commonMistake: Do not treat an agreeing trial balance as evidence that nothing is missing; the question is designed around that misconception.
